script.opening: "For a couple of months now I keep breaking out in these itchy raised welts all over — they come up, last a few hours, then vanish and pop up somewhere else. Sometimes my lips or eyelids puff up. I’ve tried changing everything — food, washing powder — but I can’t find a trigger. The itch is driving me mad. What’s causing it?"

facts.text: About 10 weeks. Itchy raised pale-pink welts, anywhere on the body, most days. Each one lasts a few hours, then goes with no mark. Has photos on her phone she can show. Not painful, no burning, no bruising afterwards.
Lips or eyelids swell about once a fortnight; goes down within a day. Never her tongue or throat; never difficulty breathing or swallowing; never fainted.
Cut out dairy, gluten and shellfish; changed washing powder and shower gel. No difference. Hot showers and tight waistbands make it worse. No new pets.
No fever, joint pains, weight loss or tiredness. No recent infections. Feels well apart from the itch. Not pregnant, not breastfeeding. No thyroid problems known.
Takes cetirizine 10 mg "only when it’s bad". Takes ibuprofen for period pains — about 5 days a month (only if asked about painkillers). No ACE inhibitors. No allergies known.
Itch worst at night — sleeping badly. Works as a hotel receptionist; embarrassed when welts appear on her neck. Married, no children.

Frustrated and tired; keen to find "the allergy". Ask: "So what am I allergic to?" Relieved to hear she can stop cutting foods out. Ask if the swelling is dangerous. Admit you only take the antihistamine when it’s bad.

ice.ideas: "It must be an allergy to something — I just need to find it."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — "I’m scared it’s a dangerous allergy and one day my throat will close up."

cues: "I can’t find a trigger" — explain spontaneous urticaria and avoid over-testing.
"Sometimes my lips or eyelids puff up" — angioedema to safety-net.
"I only take the antihistamine when it’s bad" — treatment to optimise.

checkpoints.text: Recognises CHRONIC SPONTANEOUS URTICARIA — itchy weals most days >6 weeks, each weal resolving within 24h without a mark, ± angioedema, often with no identifiable trigger
Recognises when to consider URTICARIAL VASCULITIS (weals lasting >24h, painful/burning, leaving bruising) and refers for assessment

Reassures it is usually NOT a dangerous allergy and that extensive allergy testing is unrewarding — avoiding fruitless elimination diets — while noting aggravating factors (NSAIDs, opiates, heat, pressure, stress)

Manages STEPWISE with REGULAR (not PRN) non-sedating antihistamines, UP-TITRATED to higher doses if needed, after checking pregnancy and explaining that fourfold dosing is off-label, limits tests to FBC and CRP/ESR, and refers to dermatology/immunology for refractory cases (e.g. omalizumab, NICE TA339)
Gives the ANGIOEDEMA/ANAPHYLAXIS safety-net (999 for tongue/throat swelling or breathing/swallowing difficulty) and considers ACE-inhibitor angioedema and hereditary angioedema where relevant
Addresses the frustration and the trigger-hunt, reassures appropriately, and checks understanding of the regular-antihistamine plan
Explains why allergy testing is usually unhelpful without being dismissive of her concern

Safety-nets and follows up: angioedema/airway red flags, review and up-titration/referral if not controlled, vasculitis features warranting referral, and reassurance — regular up-titrated antihistamines, not over-investigation

worked.txt: "What you’ve got is chronic urticaria — hives that come and go, each spot lasting under a day and leaving no mark, often with a bit of lip or eye swelling. The frustrating truth is that in most people there’s no specific allergy or food behind it — the body just produces them, often for months, then it settles."

"So you can stop driving yourself mad searching for a trigger — and allergy testing usually isn’t helpful here, because it’s generally not an allergy. Things like anti-inflammatory painkillers, heat, pressure and stress can flare it, but they’re not the cause."

"The key is taking a non-drowsy antihistamine REGULARLY, every day — not just when you break out. And if the standard dose isn’t enough after 2 to 4 weeks, we can increase it up to four times the usual dose, which often does the trick. That’s above the licensed dose, which is standard practice for this, and before we do I need to ask — any chance you could be pregnant, or are you breastfeeding? I’ll also check a simple blood count and inflammation marker."
"If that still doesn’t control it, I’ll refer you to the skin or allergy specialists — there are excellent further treatments, including an injection called omalizumab, for stubborn cases."
"One important safety point: the swelling is usually harmless, BUT if your TONGUE or THROAT swells, or you struggle to breathe or swallow, call 999 immediately — that’s an emergency."
"Come back if the regular antihistamine isn’t controlling it so we can increase it or refer, or if any spot lasts more than a day, becomes painful or bruises — that I’d want to look at differently."

f.learning: CHRONIC SPONTANEOUS URTICARIA is recurrent itchy WEALS (hives) occurring most days for MORE THAN 6 WEEKS, with each individual weal coming and going within 24 hours and leaving NO mark, often with ANGIOEDEMA (lip/eyelid/soft-tissue swelling) and frequently NO identifiable trigger (often idiopathic/autoimmune). If individual weals last LONGER than 24 hours, are painful/burning, or leave bruising/pigmentation, consider URTICARIAL VASCULITIS (refer dermatology for assessment/biopsy). Reassure that chronic spontaneous urticaria is usually NOT a dangerous food allergy and that extensive allergy testing is generally unrewarding — avoid fruitless elimination diets/allergy tests — while identifying aggravating (not causative) factors where relevant (NSAIDs/aspirin, opiates, heat, pressure, alcohol, stress, infection). Manage STEPWISE: regular (not just PRN) non-sedating ANTIHISTAMINES are first-line (BSACI 2015), up-titrated after 2–4 weeks to up to four times the standard dose if not controlled (international EAACI/GA²LEN/EuroGuiDerm/APAAACI guideline 2026; off-label above the licensed dose, so explain it; ask about pregnancy and breastfeeding first); limit tests to FBC and CRP or ESR; for refractory cases, refer to dermatology/immunology for add-on options (omalizumab preferred — NICE TA339 for severe disease with UAS7 of 28 or more despite antihistamine-based treatment — then ciclosporin; consider a montelukast add-on first if up-dosed antihistamine fails — BAD 2021, and a leukotriene receptor antagonist trial is required before omalizumab under TA339 — with an MHRA April 2024 neuropsychiatric warning), with short oral steroid courses only for severe flares (not long-term). Crucially counsel the angioedema/anaphylaxis safety-net — seek emergency help (999) for tongue/throat swelling or difficulty breathing/swallowing — and consider ACE-inhibitor-induced angioedema (stop the ACE inhibitor) and hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency) in recurrent isolated angioedema without weals. The skill is recognising chronic urticaria, reassuring and stopping the trigger-hunt, starting regular up-titrated antihistamines, referring if refractory/vasculitis, and giving the angioedema red-flag advice.

knowledge.guideline: [1] BSACI guideline for the management of chronic urticaria and angioedema (Powell et al., Clin Exp Allergy 2015) · [2] EAACI/GA²LEN/EuroGuiDerm/APAAACI urticaria guideline (2026 update, Allergy; international) · [3] NICE TA339 (2015) omalizumab for previously treated chronic spontaneous urticaria · [4] BNF, antihistamines · [5] MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2024), montelukast neuropsychiatric reactions
knowledge.summary: Itchy weals most days for more than 6 weeks, each lasting under 24 hours and fading without a mark, with or without angioedema, and no consistent trigger, is chronic spontaneous urticaria. It is rarely allergic. Treat with a daily non-sedating antihistamine, step it up to four times the standard dose if needed, and refer if it stays uncontrolled. Give a clear airway safety-net.

points.t: Chronic urticaria means weals, angioedema or both for more than 6 weeks [1][2]. In chronic spontaneous urticaria there is no specific external trigger; many cases are autoimmune. Inducible urticarias (pressure, cold, heat, friction, exercise) have a reproducible physical trigger and can coexist.

Individual weals that last more than 24 hours, burn or hurt rather than itch, or leave bruising or pigmentation suggest urticarial vasculitis: refer to dermatology for assessment and biopsy [1][2]. Ask about fever, joint pain and malaise alongside.

points.h: Tests: few, and not allergy panels
points.t: Routine allergy testing is not recommended when the history does not point to an allergen [1]. Limited tests only: FBC and CRP or ESR, with thyroid function and anti-TPO antibodies because thyroid autoimmunity is common in chronic spontaneous urticaria [1][2]; further tests only if the history points to them. Food elimination diets rarely help chronic spontaneous urticaria.

NSAIDs and aspirin, opioids, alcohol, heat, tight clothing, pressure, stress and intercurrent infection can make weals worse without being the cause [1]. Paracetamol is a safer analgesic choice. ACE inhibitors can cause or worsen angioedema and should be avoided in people with angioedema [1].

A second-generation non-sedating H1-antihistamine taken every day, not only on bad days [1][2]. If control is not achieved in 2–4 weeks, increase up to four times the standard dose [2]; above the licensed dose this is off-label and should be explained [4]. Avoid sedating antihistamines for regular use. A short course of oral steroid may be used for a severe flare only, never long term [1][2].

Ask before prescribing. In pregnancy, loratadine or cetirizine at the lowest effective dose is usually preferred (check UKTIS); avoid routine sedating antihistamines such as chlorphenamine. When breastfeeding, loratadine is preferred, at the lowest dose.

If uncontrolled on up-dosed antihistamine, refer to dermatology or immunology. Omalizumab is the preferred add-on [2]; NICE TA339 recommends it, in specialist care, for people aged 12 and over with severe disease (UAS7 of 28 or more) despite H1-antihistamines and a leukotriene receptor antagonist [3]. Ciclosporin is a specialist option after that [2]. UK guidance (BSACI [1]; BAD 2021) includes montelukast as an off-label add-on before omalizumab; if used, warn about neuropsychiatric effects [5].

Chronic spontaneous urticaria with angioedema is rarely anaphylaxis, but tongue or throat swelling, difficulty breathing or swallowing, a hoarse voice or collapse needs 999. Recurrent angioedema without weals raises ACE inhibitor-induced or hereditary (C1-inhibitor) angioedema, which do not respond to antihistamines [1].

model.text: Hello, Mrs Larkin, I’m Dr Shah. What’s been happening?

For a couple of months now I keep breaking out in these itchy raised welts all over. They come up, last a few hours, then vanish and pop up somewhere else. Sometimes my lips or eyelids puff up. I’ve changed everything, food, washing powder, and I can’t find a trigger. The itch is driving me mad. What’s causing it?

That sounds exhausting, especially changing so much and still not getting an answer. I’d like to ask a few questions, look at your skin, and then explain what I think is going on and what will help. Is that all right?
model.why: Acknowledges frustration and sets the agenda

model.text: Yes, please.
When a single welt comes up, how long does that one last before it fades? And does it leave any mark or bruise behind?
A few hours at most. Then it’s gone, no mark at all.
Are they itchy, or do they burn or hurt? And do you get fevers, aching joints or feel unwell with them?
Just itchy. Really itchy. I feel fine otherwise.
How often are they coming, and how is it affecting your sleep and day?
Most days. The itch is worst at night, so I’m not sleeping well.
When your lips or eyelids swell, has your tongue or throat ever swelled, or have you had any trouble breathing or swallowing, or felt faint?
No, never that. Just the lips and eyes, and it goes down.
Do any particular things set them off every time, like pressure from a waistband, cold, heat or exercise?
Not that I’ve noticed. They just appear.

Do you take any tablets, including blood-pressure tablets or painkillers like ibuprofen or aspirin? And is there any chance you could be pregnant, or are you breastfeeding? That changes which medicine I’d choose.
model.why: ACE inhibitor, NSAID aggravation and pregnancy before prescribing

model.text: Nothing regular. And no, not pregnant, not breastfeeding.
You’ve worked really hard to find a cause. What do you think is behind it, and is anything in particular worrying you?
I thought it must be an allergy to something. I’m scared it’s a dangerous one, that one day my throat will close up. I want to find the trigger and get rid of it.
That makes complete sense. Thank you for telling me. Let me take a look at your skin and then I’ll answer that worry directly.
model.why: Validates the fear and links it to the explanation

model.text: Your skin looks normal in between, with no bruising or marks, which fits what you describe: they come and go. What you have is called chronic spontaneous urticaria: hives that come most days for more than six weeks, each one lasting under a day and fading without a mark, sometimes with lip or eye swelling.
model.why: Names the diagnosis with its defining features

model.text: So what am I allergic to?

That’s the surprising part. In most people with this there’s no allergy behind it. The body’s own immune system keeps setting the hives off. That’s why changing your food and washing powder hasn’t worked, and why allergy tests usually don’t help. You haven’t missed anything.
model.why: Explains non-allergic cause and why testing is unrewarding

model.text: Really? So I can stop cutting things out?

Yes. Some things can make it flare, like anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen or aspirin, alcohol, heat, tight clothes and stress, so paracetamol is a better choice if you need a painkiller. But they aren’t the cause. I’d like to do a simple blood count and an inflammation test, and that’s all.
And the swelling? Is that dangerous?

With this condition the lip and eye swelling is very rarely the dangerous kind of allergy. It usually settles by itself. But I’ll give you clear signs to act on, so you know exactly when it would be an emergency.

The treatment that works is a non-drowsy antihistamine, for example cetirizine, taken every single day, not just when you break out. Hives are much easier to prevent than to chase. Does taking a tablet every day sound manageable?
Yes, I can do that. I’ve only been taking one when it’s bad.

If one a day isn’t controlling it after two to four weeks, we can go up, to as much as four times the usual dose. That’s higher than the leaflet says, so the leaflet may worry you, but it is standard specialist guidance and is generally well tolerated. I’ll give you a simple diary to score the hives and itch each day.
model.why: Up-dosing to fourfold explained as off-label; symptom score

model.text: And if that doesn’t work either?

Then I’d refer you to the skin or allergy specialists. There are very effective treatments for stubborn cases, including an injection called omalizumab. Most people get good control, and for many it settles on its own over months to years.
That’s a relief. I thought I’d be itching forever.

Call 999 straight away if your tongue or throat swells, if you struggle to breathe or swallow, your voice goes hoarse or you feel faint. Please also come back if any welt lasts more than a day, hurts or leaves a bruise, and I’ll see you in about four weeks with your diary to decide whether to increase the dose.
model.why: Airway 999 advice, vasculitis features, planned review

model.text: Okay.
Just so I know I’ve explained it well, how would you describe the plan to someone at home?
It’s not an allergy, so stop hunting for triggers. Take the antihistamine every day, increase it if you say so, avoid ibuprofen, and 999 if my throat swells.
That’s exactly it. You’ve done nothing wrong. We’ll get this under control together.

social.t: Night itch disturbs sleep and concentration. Ask about work and home impact; a non-sedating daily dose avoids daytime drowsiness at work or when driving.
Unnecessary elimination diets cost time and money and can restrict nutrition. Ending them is part of the treatment.

legal.t: Up-dosing an antihistamine above the licensed dose is off-label. GMC Good practice in proposing, prescribing, providing and managing medicines and devices (2021): explain this, record the reason and the discussion.
Sedating antihistamines can impair driving. Choose non-sedating ones and advise not to drive if drowsy after a dose increase.

professional.t: Allergy panels in chronic spontaneous urticaria create false positives and false leads. Explaining why you are not testing is good practice, not dismissal.
Say plainly that the cause is internal and the course is unpredictable, but usually improves; offer a clear review plan.

community.t: Community pharmacists can advise on antihistamine timing and interactions. Allergy UK has patient information on urticaria and angioedema.

redFlags: Tongue or throat swelling, breathing or swallowing difficulty, hoarse voice, collapse (999)
Weals lasting more than 24 hours, painful or leaving bruising (urticarial vasculitis)
Angioedema without weals, or on an ACE inhibitor (bradykinin angioedema)
psychosocial: Exhausting trigger hunt and restricted diet
Fear of a sudden severe reaction
ice: Idea: an allergy to something she eats or uses
Concern: that it is dangerous and her throat will close
Expectation: to find the trigger and cure it

playbook.diagnosis: “This is chronic spontaneous urticaria: hives most days for over six weeks, each lasting under a day, sometimes with lip or eye swelling. It usually isn’t caused by an allergy.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of the skin’s itch cells as a smoke alarm that has become oversensitive. It goes off without any real fire. There’s nothing to find in your food or washing powder. The antihistamine turns the alarm’s sensitivity down.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought this was a dangerous allergy and have been trying hard to find the trigger. The good news is it usually isn’t an allergy, so you can stop searching. And I’ll show you exactly which swellings would be an emergency.”
management.psychosocial: End the elimination diets, address sleep, and make daily dosing practical; explain the off-label step-up so the leaflet doesn’t alarm her.
sharedPlan: Daily second-generation non-sedating antihistamine (choice and dose per BNF; pregnancy status checked)
If not controlled after 2–4 weeks, increase up to four times the standard dose (off-label, explained)
FBC, CRP or ESR and thyroid tests only; no allergy panel
Paracetamol rather than NSAIDs; symptom diary
Refer to dermatology or immunology if uncontrolled (omalizumab, NICE TA339)
safetyNet: 999 for tongue or throat swelling, breathing or swallowing difficulty, hoarse voice or faintness
Return if a weal lasts more than 24 hours, hurts or bruises
Review in about 4 weeks with the diary to decide on up-dosing or referral

pitfalls.intro: This station is lost by chasing an allergy that isn’t there, by as-needed antihistamines, and by a missing airway safety-net. Each pattern below is common and fixable.

items.fail: Ordering an allergy panel or advising a strict elimination diet.
items.why: BSACI 2015: allergy testing is not recommended in chronic spontaneous urticaria without a suggestive history; it produces false leads.
items.fix: Explain why testing won’t help; FBC, CRP or ESR and thyroid tests only.

items.fail: Prescribing an antihistamine to take “when the hives come”.
items.why: Regular daily dosing is first-line in BSACI and international guidance.
items.fix: Daily dose, with a planned step-up to four times the standard dose if not controlled after 2–4 weeks.

items.fail: Never asking how long a single weal lasts or whether it bruises.
items.why: Weals over 24 hours, painful or bruising, suggest urticarial vasculitis needing dermatology.
items.fix: Ask the 24-hour question and include it in the safety-net.

items.fail: Up-dosing without checking pregnancy, or without explaining that it is off-label.
items.why: Drug choice changes in pregnancy (BSACI 2015) and the leaflet will contradict the plan.
items.fix: Ask about pregnancy and breastfeeding; explain the off-label step-up and record it.

items.fail: Dismissing the trigger hunt: “there’s no point doing all that”.
items.why: She has invested a lot; dismissal loses trust.
items.fix: Acknowledge the effort, then explain why the cause is internal: “You haven’t missed anything.”

items.why: No airway safety-net is a safety failure.
items.fix: 999 for tongue or throat swelling, breathing or swallowing difficulty; teach-back to confirm.

avoid.instead: “In most people with this there isn’t an allergy behind it, so allergy tests rarely help.”
avoid.why: BSACI 2015: routine allergy testing is not recommended in chronic spontaneous urticaria without a suggestive history.

SCA_MODELS.text: So what am I allergic to?

That’s the surprising part. In most people with this there’s no allergy behind it. The body’s own immune system keeps setting the hives off. That’s why changing your food and washing powder hasn’t worked, and why allergy tests usually don’t help. You haven’t missed anything.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains non-allergic cause and why testing is unrewarding

SCA_MODELS.text: Really? So I can stop cutting things out?

Yes. Some things can make it flare, like anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen or aspirin, alcohol, heat, tight clothes and stress, so paracetamol is a better choice if you need a painkiller. But they aren’t the cause. I’d like to do a simple blood count and an inflammation test, and that’s all.
And the swelling? Is that dangerous?

With this condition the lip and eye swelling is very rarely the dangerous kind of allergy. It usually settles by itself. But I’ll give you clear signs to act on, so you know exactly when it would be an emergency.

The treatment that works is a non-drowsy antihistamine, for example cetirizine, taken every single day, not just when you break out. Hives are much easier to prevent than to chase. Does taking a tablet every day sound manageable?
Yes, I can do that. I’ve only been taking one when it’s bad.

If one a day isn’t controlling it after two to four weeks, we can go up, to as much as four times the usual dose. That’s higher than the leaflet says, so the leaflet may worry you, but it is standard specialist guidance and is generally well tolerated. I’ll give you a simple diary to score the hives and itch each day.
SCA_MODELS.why: Up-dosing to fourfold explained as off-label; symptom score

SCA_MODELS.text: And if that doesn’t work either?

Then I’d refer you to the skin or allergy specialists. There are very effective treatments for stubborn cases, including an injection called omalizumab. Most people get good control, and for many it settles on its own over months to years.
That’s a relief. I thought I’d be itching forever.

Call 999 straight away if your tongue or throat swells, if you struggle to breathe or swallow, your voice goes hoarse or you feel faint. Please also come back if any welt lasts more than a day, hurts or leaves a bruise, and I’ll see you in about four weeks with your diary to decide whether to increase the dose.
SCA_MODELS.why: Airway 999 advice, vasculitis features, planned review

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay.
Just so I know I’ve explained it well, how would you describe the plan to someone at home?
It’s not an allergy, so stop hunting for triggers. Take the antihistamine every day, increase it if you say so, avoid ibuprofen, and 999 if my throat swells.
That’s exactly it. You’ve done nothing wrong. We’ll get this under control together.

SCA_STEM.name: Sofia Larkin
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: No previous consultations about a rash recorded. No allergy tests on file.
SCA_STEM.reason: Itchy raised welts most days for a couple of months, sometimes with lip or eyelid swelling. Cannot find a trigger.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] BSACI guideline for the management of chronic urticaria and angioedema (Powell et al., Clin Exp Allergy 2015) · [2] EAACI/GA²LEN/EuroGuiDerm/APAAACI urticaria guideline (2026 update, Allergy; international) · [3] NICE TA339 (2015) omalizumab for previously treated chronic spontaneous urticaria · [4] BNF, antihistamines · [5] MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2024), montelukast neuropsychiatric reactions
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Itchy weals most days for more than 6 weeks, each lasting under 24 hours and fading without a mark, with or without angioedema, and no consistent trigger, is chronic spontaneous urticaria. It is rarely allergic. Treat with a daily non-sedating antihistamine, step it up to four times the standard dose if needed, and refer if it stays uncontrolled. Give a clear airway safety-net.

points.t: Chronic urticaria means weals, angioedema or both for more than 6 weeks [1][2]. In chronic spontaneous urticaria there is no specific external trigger; many cases are autoimmune. Inducible urticarias (pressure, cold, heat, friction, exercise) have a reproducible physical trigger and can coexist.

Individual weals that last more than 24 hours, burn or hurt rather than itch, or leave bruising or pigmentation suggest urticarial vasculitis: refer to dermatology for assessment and biopsy [1][2]. Ask about fever, joint pain and malaise alongside.

points.h: Tests: few, and not allergy panels
points.t: Routine allergy testing is not recommended when the history does not point to an allergen [1]. Limited tests only: FBC and CRP or ESR, with thyroid function and anti-TPO antibodies because thyroid autoimmunity is common in chronic spontaneous urticaria [1][2]; further tests only if the history points to them. Food elimination diets rarely help chronic spontaneous urticaria.

NSAIDs and aspirin, opioids, alcohol, heat, tight clothing, pressure, stress and intercurrent infection can make weals worse without being the cause [1]. Paracetamol is a safer analgesic choice. ACE inhibitors can cause or worsen angioedema and should be avoided in people with angioedema [1].

A second-generation non-sedating H1-antihistamine taken every day, not only on bad days [1][2]. If control is not achieved in 2–4 weeks, increase up to four times the standard dose [2]; above the licensed dose this is off-label and should be explained [4]. Avoid sedating antihistamines for regular use. A short course of oral steroid may be used for a severe flare only, never long term [1][2].

Ask before prescribing. In pregnancy, loratadine or cetirizine at the lowest effective dose is usually preferred (check UKTIS); avoid routine sedating antihistamines such as chlorphenamine. When breastfeeding, loratadine is preferred, at the lowest dose.

If uncontrolled on up-dosed antihistamine, refer to dermatology or immunology. Omalizumab is the preferred add-on [2]; NICE TA339 recommends it, in specialist care, for people aged 12 and over with severe disease (UAS7 of 28 or more) despite H1-antihistamines and a leukotriene receptor antagonist [3]. Ciclosporin is a specialist option after that [2]. UK guidance (BSACI [1]; BAD 2021) includes montelukast as an off-label add-on before omalizumab; if used, warn about neuropsychiatric effects [5].

Chronic spontaneous urticaria with angioedema is rarely anaphylaxis, but tongue or throat swelling, difficulty breathing or swallowing, a hoarse voice or collapse needs 999. Recurrent angioedema without weals raises ACE inhibitor-induced or hereditary (C1-inhibitor) angioedema, which do not respond to antihistamines [1].

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her describe the transient itchy weals, the lip and eyelid swelling and the failed trigger hunt.
Sleep loss from night itch; the effort spent changing food and products; impact on daily life.
Picked up the swelling episodes and asked directly about tongue, throat and breathing; heard the frustration behind “I can’t find a trigger”.
Idea (an allergy), concern (a dangerous reaction, her throat closing), expectation (find and remove the trigger).
Examines the skin; checks weal duration and bruising; FBC, CRP or ESR and thyroid tests only; no allergy panel.
Chronic spontaneous versus inducible urticaria, urticarial vasculitis, drug-induced (NSAID, ACE inhibitor) and hereditary angioedema.
Screened for airway compromise, systemic features and weals lasting more than 24 hours.
Chronic spontaneous urticaria with angioedema, not allergic.
Daily second-generation antihistamine, up to four times the dose after 2–4 weeks if needed (off-label explained); pregnancy checked before prescribing; paracetamol rather than NSAIDs.
Stops fruitless elimination diets; addresses sleep; referral for omalizumab if refractory; short steroid course only for severe flares.
999 for tongue or throat swelling or breathing difficulty; return for weals lasting over 24 hours or bruising; review in about 4 weeks with a symptom diary.

social.t: Night itch disturbs sleep and concentration. Ask about work and home impact; a non-sedating daily dose avoids daytime drowsiness at work or when driving.
Unnecessary elimination diets cost time and money and can restrict nutrition. Ending them is part of the treatment.

legal.t: Up-dosing an antihistamine above the licensed dose is off-label. GMC Good practice in proposing, prescribing, providing and managing medicines and devices (2021): explain this, record the reason and the discussion.
Sedating antihistamines can impair driving. Choose non-sedating ones and advise not to drive if drowsy after a dose increase.

professional.t: Allergy panels in chronic spontaneous urticaria create false positives and false leads. Explaining why you are not testing is good practice, not dismissal.
Say plainly that the cause is internal and the course is unpredictable, but usually improves; offer a clear review plan.

community.t: Community pharmacists can advise on antihistamine timing and interactions. Allergy UK has patient information on urticaria and angioedema.

redFlags: Tongue or throat swelling, breathing or swallowing difficulty, hoarse voice, collapse (999)
Weals lasting more than 24 hours, painful or leaving bruising (urticarial vasculitis)
Angioedema without weals, or on an ACE inhibitor (bradykinin angioedema)
psychosocial: Exhausting trigger hunt and restricted diet
Fear of a sudden severe reaction
ice: Idea: an allergy to something she eats or uses
Concern: that it is dangerous and her throat will close
Expectation: to find the trigger and cure it

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is chronic spontaneous urticaria: hives most days for over six weeks, each lasting under a day, sometimes with lip or eye swelling. It usually isn’t caused by an allergy.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of the skin’s itch cells as a smoke alarm that has become oversensitive. It goes off without any real fire. There’s nothing to find in your food or washing powder. The antihistamine turns the alarm’s sensitivity down.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought this was a dangerous allergy and have been trying hard to find the trigger. The good news is it usually isn’t an allergy, so you can stop searching. And I’ll show you exactly which swellings would be an emergency.”
management.psychosocial: End the elimination diets, address sleep, and make daily dosing practical; explain the off-label step-up so the leaflet doesn’t alarm her.
sharedPlan: Daily second-generation non-sedating antihistamine (choice and dose per BNF; pregnancy status checked)
If not controlled after 2–4 weeks, increase up to four times the standard dose (off-label, explained)
FBC, CRP or ESR and thyroid tests only; no allergy panel
Paracetamol rather than NSAIDs; symptom diary
Refer to dermatology or immunology if uncontrolled (omalizumab, NICE TA339)
safetyNet: 999 for tongue or throat swelling, breathing or swallowing difficulty, hoarse voice or faintness
Return if a weal lasts more than 24 hours, hurts or bruises
Review in about 4 weeks with the diary to decide on up-dosing or referral

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is lost by chasing an allergy that isn’t there, by as-needed antihistamines, and by a missing airway safety-net. Each pattern below is common and fixable.

items.fail: Ordering an allergy panel or advising a strict elimination diet.
items.why: BSACI 2015: allergy testing is not recommended in chronic spontaneous urticaria without a suggestive history; it produces false leads.
items.fix: Explain why testing won’t help; FBC, CRP or ESR and thyroid tests only.

items.fail: Prescribing an antihistamine to take “when the hives come”.
items.why: Regular daily dosing is first-line in BSACI and international guidance.
items.fix: Daily dose, with a planned step-up to four times the standard dose if not controlled after 2–4 weeks.

items.fail: Never asking how long a single weal lasts or whether it bruises.
items.why: Weals over 24 hours, painful or bruising, suggest urticarial vasculitis needing dermatology.
items.fix: Ask the 24-hour question and include it in the safety-net.

items.fail: Up-dosing without checking pregnancy, or without explaining that it is off-label.
items.why: Drug choice changes in pregnancy (BSACI 2015) and the leaflet will contradict the plan.
items.fix: Ask about pregnancy and breastfeeding; explain the off-label step-up and record it.

items.fail: Dismissing the trigger hunt: “there’s no point doing all that”.
items.why: She has invested a lot; dismissal loses trust.
items.fix: Acknowledge the effort, then explain why the cause is internal: “You haven’t missed anything.”

items.why: No airway safety-net is a safety failure.
items.fix: 999 for tongue or throat swelling, breathing or swallowing difficulty; teach-back to confirm.
